subject: MGMT160
title: Management in Practice: Advice, Evidence and Your Development Plan

questions.stem: Explain advice 9, 'use AI like a careful professional'.
options: Use it to speed up routine work and verify everything before it goes out under your name
Avoid AI completely, because professionals are judged on what they can do without it and employers know the difference
Copy AI output to save time, because the tools are now accurate enough to trust
Use AI only for homework, where a mistake costs nothing but a mark
questions.why: Careful users thrive; fast copiers get caught. See §10.2.

questions.stem: Describe the 'friend's mistake' scenario in the chapter.
options: A friend asks you to hide a mistake that cost money; the strong move is to stand beside them while they tell it
A friend asks for a loan to cover a mistake at work, and the strong move is to lend the money without telling anyone else about it
A friend wants your notes for a report, and the strong move is to share them but insist on credit
A friend wants to lead the project, and the strong move is to let them and support them from behind
questions.why: Mistakes are forgivable; cover-ups end careers. See §10.3.

questions.stem: Explain why the chapter says 'influence is leadership; the title is paperwork'.
options: You can lead a group by proposing a plan and roles without being appointed
Titles are not real, so nobody should take an organisation chart seriously
Only appointed leaders can lead, so a group without a leader should ask for one
Paperwork is leadership, because the person who writes the plan controls the group
questions.why: The first leadership moment needs no title. See §10.3.

questions.stem: Describe the weak move in the first leadership moment.
options: Waiting for someone to be appointed while nothing gets done
Proposing a simple plan with tasks, owners and dates before anyone has agreed to it
Asking each person which piece they want instead of assigning the work
Setting a weekly check on the group
questions.why: Waiting is the weak move. See §10.3.

questions.stem: Describe Roselinde Torres's third question for leaders.
options: Are you courageous enough to abandon what made you successful?
How much do you earn compared with the people you lead?
How many people report to you directly and indirectly?
Do you have an MBA or an equivalent qualification in management?
questions.why: Nokia failed this question. See §10.5.

questions.stem: Explain why the chapter says to watch Drew Dudley's talk first.
options: It captures the chapter's spirit — leadership is small moments that change someone's direction
It is the shortest of the videos, so it fits before the lecture begins without delaying the rest of the class
It is about salaries, which is what students most want to know about management
It explains KPIs, which students need before they can follow the other talks
questions.why: The lollipop moment. See §10.5.

questions.stem: Describe a one-minute goal.
options: Agreeing what good looks like before the work starts
A goal that takes one minute to reach, so that the employee has an early success
A goal set once a year and reviewed at appraisal
A goal nobody writes down, because writing it down makes it too formal
questions.why: Agree what good looks like first. See §10.6.

questions.stem: Describe a one-minute praising.
options: Catching someone doing something right and saying so, promptly and specifically
A yearly bonus paid to the employee with the best results
A public ranking of the team updated every week on the noticeboard
A long speech at the team meeting thanking everyone for their effort during the year
questions.why: Catch people doing something right. See §10.6.

questions.stem: Explain why the chapter lists six studies.
options: To show that the course's advice rests on evidence, not opinion
To make the exam longer and harder for students who have not read the chapter
Because university courses are required to cite a minimum number of studies
To replace the textbook, which the chapter says is out of date
questions.why: Evidence, not opinion. See §10.7.

questions.stem: Describe what Tversky and Kahneman found.
options: Bias is built into all minds, so systems must be designed against it
Only some people are biased
Experts are never biased, because experience corrects the errors of intuition
Bias can be removed by trying harder to be objective when making decisions
questions.why: Design against bias. See §10.7.

questions.stem: Describe the habit of checking.
options: Verifying claims, numbers and sources before acting or signing
Checking the clock so that every task finishes on time
Reviewing colleagues' work for mistakes so that they can be reported to the manager
Checking social media to see what customers are saying about the company
questions.why: One of the three things no dataset contains. See §10.7.

questions.stem: Describe what the two lowest rows of the scorecard are for.
options: They are the input for your development plan
They are failures to hide from the professor and from future employers
They decide your exam grade, so they should be scored as high as possible
They are ignored, because a plan should build on strengths rather than weaknesses
questions.why: Your two lowest rows are inputs, not failures. See §10.8.

questions.stem: Explain the phrase 'you are your own first employee'.
options: Managing yourself uses the same tools as managing a team: goals, resources, motivation, a checkpoint
You should pay yourself a salary from your student budget every month to learn financial discipline early in life
You should hire yourself for a role you want before anyone else offers it to you
Employees should manage themselves, so that managers are no longer needed
questions.why: Manage yourself with the course's tools. See §10.8.

questions.stem: Determine the advice behind a manager who asks 'why?' before acting on a complaint.
options: Advice 1 — diagnose before you act
Advice 6 — lead small things
Advice 9 — use AI like a careful professional
Advice 10 — stay a student after the course ends
questions.why: The visible problem is usually the symptom. See §10.1.

questions.stem: Select the goal that follows advice 2.
options: Raise my average mark from 68 to 75 by the end of the semester
Do better this semester than I did last semester in every subject
Try harder in the subjects where I know I have been weak
Be a good student who attends every class and hands in every assignment
questions.why: Numbers and dates. See §10.1.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who corrects an employee in front of the whole team. Determine the advice broken.
options: Advice 4 — praise specifically, correct privately
Advice 2 — write goals with numbers and dates
Advice 5 — run the four questions on small choices
Advice 9 — use AI like a careful professional
questions.why: Correct privately, about the work. See §10.1.

questions.stem: Select the strong move when your group project has no leader and nothing done.
options: Propose a simple plan with tasks, owners and dates, and ask each person which piece they want
Wait for the professor to appoint someone, since the group has no authority to choose
Do everything yourself and put everyone's name on it, because that is faster than organising people
Leave the group and ask to join one that has already started working
questions.why: Lead without announcing it. See §10.3.

questions.stem: Determine the chapter's reason for not hiding a friend's costly mistake.
options: It fails the fairness, harm and public tests, and cover-ups end careers
Friends should always be reported
Mistakes are never forgivable, so the friend will be dismissed either way
The manager will find out anyway, so hiding it only delays the consequences
questions.why: Mistakes are forgivable; cover-ups are not. See §10.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a student who argues loudly in a meeting when a senior person dismisses her idea. Determine the better move.
options: Afterwards, privately, offer five minutes with the numbers behind the idea
Argue louder in the meeting until the senior person finally agrees to listen to the idea
Give up the idea, because a senior person's judgement is usually right
Email the senior person's boss with the idea and the evidence behind it
questions.why: Evidence decides, not volume. See §10.4.

questions.stem: Determine what Dan Pink's talk implies for a manager who offers bigger bonuses for creative work.
options: Bigger rewards can worsen thinking work; autonomy, mastery and purpose drive it
Bigger bonuses always help
Creative work needs strict supervision, because creative people lose focus without it
Bonuses are the only motivator that works for every kind of work and every person
questions.why: Autonomy, mastery, purpose. See §10.5.

questions.stem: Select the course company that answered Torres's third question well.
options: Emirates — adapted after its first loss and returned to record profits
Nokia — kept perfecting yesterday's phone
Kodak — protected film against the digital camera it had invented itself
A café that never changed its menu and kept its loyal customers for thirty years
questions.why: Emirates adapted; Nokia and Kodak did not. See §10.5 and Chapter 3.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who gives feedback only at the annual review. Determine the One Minute Manager's advice.
options: Give short, prompt praisings and redirects when the behaviour happens
Wait for the annual review to give feedback
Write a longer review so that every point of the year is covered properly
Skip feedback altogether, because adults do not need to be told how they are doing
questions.why: Minutes, not hours; promptly. See §10.6.

questions.stem: Determine the implication of the six studies for what to build at university.
options: Judgement under uncertainty, the ability to create safety, and the habit of checking
Typing speed and the ability to memorise rules and procedures
Only technical software skills, because that is what employers test for
Nothing — the studies are history and the world of work has moved on so far that they no longer apply
questions.why: No dataset contains these three. See §10.7.

questions.stem: Analyse a team that reports more errors than another. Determine Edmondson's reading.
options: It may be the better team — members feel safe to report instead of hiding
It is the worse team, because it is making more mistakes than the other
Errors should be punished, so the team with more reports needs stricter management
Reporting should stop, because a team that reports many errors looks bad to the organisation
questions.why: Teams that report learn faster. See §10.7 and §10.6.

questions.stem: Select the checkpoint for a development plan written in September.
options: Re-take the scorecard in December and compare
Never check, because a plan should be trusted once it has been written
Check every hour, because frequent control is the only way to stay on track
Ask a friend to guess how far you have progressed and accept their estimate
questions.why: A plan without a checkpoint is a wish. See §10.8.

questions.stem: Classify a development goal with no number, no date and no how.
options: A wish, not a goal
A SMART goal, because it describes what the student wants
A checkpoint, because it marks where the student wants to be
A resource, because it tells the student what to work on
questions.why: Practise what you teach yourself. See §10.8.
